turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am afraid I do not approve of women who go about very little, Mr. Worthing. It suggests a lack of engagement with society, which is most unsatisfactory. Now, tell me about your relations with the criminal class.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, surely you cannot speak of Jack in such a manner! He is a gentleman of the highest moral standards.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, I must insist that your acquaintanceship with the criminal class is a matter of grave concern. However, I shall overlook it for now, Gwendolen’s sake.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I am deeply sorry, Lady Bracknell, if my past associations have caused any concern. I assure you that I have since distanced myself from such influences and am fully committed to upholding the highest standards of conduct.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I appreciate your assurances, Mr. Worthing, but actions speak louder than words. Let us move on to more pressing matters. Tell me, what are your views on marriage?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I hold marriage in the highest regard and believe it to be the foundation of a stable and prosperous society.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Indeed, Mr. Worthing, marriage is a serious matter. Your views are commendable, but they must be accompanied by a suitable social standing and financial stability. Can you assure me of your ability to provide for a wife and ensure her place in the best circles of society?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I am in possession of a comfortable income and have inherited a country estate, which I am certain will provide Gwendolen with everything she deserves and more.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I see, Mr. Worthing. It is reassuring to hear that you possess both the means and the inclination to maintain the social status to which my daughter is accustomed. However, I must ask: can you provide references to your family background and connections within high society?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand your concerns, Lady Bracknell. While my immediate family is modest, I have made it my mission to associate with the finest individuals in society and have garnered respect and friendships among them.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, while your financial standing is satisfactory, the absence of a notable family background is a significant drawback. I must ask, do you have any connections to the nobility or influential families that could elevate your status in society?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I respect your requirements and understand the importance of family connections. Though I may not come from a lineage of nobles, I have dedicated myself to becoming a gentleman of the highest regard, and I believe I can offer Gwendolen a future filled with happiness and respectability.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, while your efforts to elevate yourself are commendable, the lack of a distinguished pedigree remains a substantial obstacle. I must inquire, do you have any plans to acquire a more illustrious lineage through marriage or other means?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I appreciate your concern for Gwendolen's future. I am committed to earning a respectable standing through my own merit and have no plans to marry into a more illustrious lineage. My intention is to provide Gwendolen with a life of happiness and security, founded on mutual love and respect.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, your dedication is clear, but it is my duty to ensure that Gwendolen marries into a family with a solid reputation and heritage. I fear your aspirations, commendable though they may be, do not align with the expectations of our society.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I understand your perspective and the importance you place on heritage and reputation. My hope is that through my actions and character, I can earn the respect and approval of your family and society.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, while your ambitions are evident, I must remind you that in our society, one's birth and connections often speak louder than one's personal merits. Your future actions must not only demonstrate your character but also align with the expectations set by our social circles.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I respect the values and expectations of your society. I assure you that I will strive to uphold them while also fostering a relationship based on genuine affection and mutual respect.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, your assurances are noted. However, I must emphasize that actions speak louder than words. It is imperative that you demonstrate your capacity to meet our society's expectations in tangible ways. Until then, I shall reserve final judgment.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I appreciate your guidance and the high standards you uphold. I promise to work diligently to prove myself worthy of Gwendolen's hand in marriage and your family's esteem.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I dons depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
